newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels give U.N. 60 days to repatriate refugees.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels give U.N. 60 days to repatriate refugees.

text.p: Zaire's rebel leader Laurent Kabila on Sunday gave the United Nations 60 days to repatriate all Rwandan Hutu refugees remaining in Zaire or he would do the job himself.
"This has gone on for too long and if it is not completed, we will do it ourselves," he told a news conference after an afternoon of meetings with senior United Nations and European Union officials.
"I have given them 60 days to get this problem sorted out. It must be done."

Kabila also strenuously denied his forces were responsible for attacking over 50,000 refugees and sparking their flight last week from makeshift camps about 35 kilometers (22 miles) south of Kisangani.
He said he would be seeking a personal apology from U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan who on Thursday described the fate of the refugees as "slow extermination".
"The United Nations has made promises it has not kept and Kofi Annan must come here himself to apologise," said Kabila.
Kabila said he had been assured by U.N. officials in Kisangani that nothing they had reported to their headquarters should have prompted Annan's robust criticisms.
U.N. officials were not immediately available for comment.
Sunday's breakthrough comes six days after rebel authorities began a lock-out of the area containing the refugees camps and stopped aid organisations or journalists from entering them.
When U.N. officials finally managed to visit the camps on Wednesday, they found the more than 50,000 inhabitants had fled -- seemingly in haste -- and airsweeps of the area have failed to find them.
Around 50 refugees who made their way to Kisangani on Saturday told of the camp being surrounded on Tuesday by soldiers and then being attacked by villagers armed with axes and machetes.

Some of them were among 33 refugees who were airlifted from Kisangani to Kigali on Sunday afternoon -- the first such evacuation since the U.N. approved an unprecedented air evacuation earlier this month.
United Nations officials said a great deal of work still remained to be done to successfully repatriate those remaining, but they were optimistic following asurances from Kabila.
Aldo Ajello, the EU's special envoy to the Great Lakes, told Reuters: "I'm very happy with the assurances I have been given. I hope we can get moving soon."
Kabila said his forces knew where the bulk of the refugees from Kasese camp had fled to and he would help the U.N. locate them. "They can go now if they want," he said.

Some refugees played a prominent role in the 1994 slaughter of an estimated 800,000 minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus in Rwanda, and Kabila told Reuters last week that criminals among them had transported their lawlessness to Zaire.
Refugees among those who crossed the river on Saturday could not give a clear picture of what happened to make them flee.
The 50,000-plus refugees at Kasese, about 35 km (22 miles) south of Kisangani, were among the last of over a million Hutus who fled Rwanda in 1994 to escape reprisal for the genocide.

Most returned in a huge wave of repatriation sparked by Kabila's sweeping rebel advance through eastern Zaire. This group instead marched nearly 500 kms (300 miles) west through dense jungle before being overwhelmed by hunger, exhaustion and illness just south of Kisangani.
It was there that the rebel army overtook them.
An outbreak of cholera was cited by rebels as the reason for delaying the start of a planned U.N. airlift of the refugees.
Rebel authorities have blamed local hostility to the refugees on envy sparked by the sight of tonnes of food and other aid being given to them by aid organisations.
Local Zaireans have looted U.N. warehouses and a train carrying supplies to the camps, but some of them said they had been urged on by rebel soldiers.
